name: Femur
fact: The femur forms the thigh; its head articulates with the acetabulum at the hip.
question: What bone forms the thigh?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Transmits body weight between hip and knee and provides leverage for thigh muscles.
description: The femur is the longest and strongest bone of the human skeleton. Its rounded head meets the acetabulum; the neck joins the shaft, which ends in medial and lateral condyles that participate in the knee joint.
relationships: Hip bone, patella, tibia, quadriceps and hamstring attachment sites.
study_tip: Find the head, neck, greater trochanter and distal condyles; compare the anterior and posterior views.
short: The femur forms the thigh; its head articulates with the acetabulum at the hip.

name: Tibia
fact: The tibia is the larger, medial, primary weight-bearing bone of the leg.
question: Which lower-leg bone bears most body weight?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Bears most of the leg's weight and forms the medial ankle.
description: The tibia is the large medial bone of the leg. Its proximal condyles meet the femur at the knee; its distal medial malleolus forms the inner ankle. It participates in the ankle joint with the talus.
relationships: Femur, fibula, talus, patellar ligament, interosseous membrane.
study_tip: Locate the tibial tuberosity, anterior crest and medial malleolus.
short: The tibia is the larger, medial, primary weight-bearing bone of the leg.

name: Fibula
fact: The fibula is the slender lateral bone of the leg.
question: Which lower-leg bone is lateral?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Provides lateral ankle stability and attachment for muscles; it bears relatively little body weight.
description: The fibula is the slender lateral bone of the lower leg. Its head lies near the knee, while its distal end forms the lateral malleolus. It does not articulate directly with the femur.
relationships: Tibia, talus, interosseous membrane and lateral ankle ligaments.
study_tip: Compare medial tibia with lateral fibula and identify the lateral malleolus.
short: The fibula is the slender lateral bone of the leg.

name: Patella
fact: The patella is a sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps tendon.
question: What is the anatomical term for the kneecap?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Improves the mechanical leverage of the quadriceps tendon over the knee.
description: The patella is a sesamoid bone within the knee extensor mechanism. Its posterior articular surface glides against the femur as the knee bends and straightens.
relationships: Quadriceps tendon, patellar ligament, distal femur and proximal tibia.
study_tip: Locate the apex inferiorly and the broad base superiorly.
short: The patella is a sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps tendon.

name: Humerus
fact: The humerus is the long bone of the arm between shoulder and elbow.
question: Which bone extends from the shoulder to the elbow?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Acts as the upper arm's bony lever for shoulder and elbow movements.
description: The humerus extends from the shoulder to the elbow. The proximal head articulates with the scapular glenoid, and the distal trochlea and capitulum articulate with ulna and radius.
relationships: Scapula, radius, ulna, deltoid insertion and rotator-cuff tendons.
study_tip: Identify the head, greater tubercle, deltoid tuberosity and distal epicondyles.
short: The humerus is the long bone of the arm between shoulder and elbow.

name: Radius
fact: In anatomical position, the radius is the lateral bone of the forearm, on the thumb side.
question: Which forearm bone is lateral in anatomical position?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Allows pronation and supination with the ulna and transfers loads through the wrist.
description: The radius is the lateral forearm bone in anatomical position (thumb side). Its head rotates near the elbow and the broad distal end meets carpal bones at the wrist.
relationships: Ulna, humerus, scaphoid, lunate and interosseous membrane.
study_tip: Rotate to anatomical position and distinguish thumb-side radius from the ulna.
short: In anatomical position, the radius is the lateral bone of the forearm, on the thumb side.

name: Ulna
fact: In anatomical position, the ulna is the medial forearm bone.
question: Which forearm bone is medial in anatomical position?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Stabilizes the elbow and acts as a pivot partner for forearm rotation.
description: The ulna lies medially in anatomical position (little-finger side). Its olecranon forms the point of the elbow; the trochlear notch articulates with the humerus.
relationships: Radius, trochlea of humerus, olecranon, interosseous membrane.
study_tip: Identify olecranon and coronoid process; compare the narrow distal and broad proximal ends.
short: In anatomical position, the ulna is the medial forearm bone.

name: Scapula
fact: The scapula is the shoulder blade; its glenoid cavity articulates with the humeral head.
question: Which bone contains the glenoid cavity?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Provides muscle attachments and the socket for shoulder movement.
description: The scapula is a flat triangular shoulder-girdle bone on the posterior thorax. The glenoid cavity articulates with the humeral head and the acromion connects with the clavicle.
relationships: Clavicle, humerus, rotator-cuff muscles, serratus anterior, trapezius.
study_tip: Locate scapular spine, acromion, coracoid process and glenoid cavity.
short: The scapula is the shoulder blade; its glenoid cavity articulates with the humeral head.

name: Clavicle
fact: The clavicle is the collarbone and articulates with the sternum and scapula.
question: What is the anatomical name of the collarbone?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Braces the shoulder laterally away from the thorax and transfers upper-limb forces.
description: The clavicle is an S-shaped bone between the sternum and acromion of the scapula. Its medial sternoclavicular and lateral acromioclavicular articulations connect upper limb and trunk.
relationships: Manubrium, acromion, sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints.
study_tip: Identify the thicker sternal and flatter acromial ends.
short: The clavicle is the collarbone and articulates with the sternum and scapula.

name: Sternum
fact: The sternum is the breastbone on the anterior midline of the thorax.
question: What is the breastbone called?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Protects anterior thoracic structures and anchors the ribs and clavicles.
description: The sternum lies along the anterior midline of the chest. Its three main parts are the manubrium, body and xiphoid process; costal cartilages link most true ribs to it.
relationships: Clavicles, costal cartilages, ribs and anterior thoracic wall.
study_tip: Find the jugular notch, manubriosternal junction (sternal angle) and xiphoid.
short: The sternum is the breastbone on the anterior midline of the thorax.

name: Mandible
fact: The mandible forms the lower jaw and articulates with the temporal bones.
question: Which bone forms the lower jaw?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Supports the lower teeth and moves during chewing and speech.
description: The mandible is the movable lower-jaw bone. Its condylar processes articulate with temporal bones, forming temporomandibular joints; the coronoid processes anchor temporalis muscles.
relationships: Temporal bones, teeth, masseter and temporalis muscles.
study_tip: Find the body, ramus, angle, condylar and coronoid processes.
short: The mandible forms the lower jaw and articulates with the temporal bones.

name: Occipital bone
fact: The occipital bone is in the posterior skull and contains the foramen magnum.
question: Which skull bone contains the foramen magnum?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Protects the back of the brain and transmits the spinal cord through the foramen magnum.
description: The occipital bone forms much of the posterior and inferior skull. Its large foramen magnum surrounds the transition from medulla to spinal cord and its condyles articulate with atlas (C1).
relationships: Parietal and temporal bones, atlas and posterior neck muscles.
study_tip: Rotate beneath the skull to locate the foramen magnum and occipital condyles.
short: The occipital bone is in the posterior skull and contains the foramen magnum.

name: Frontal bone
fact: The frontal bone forms the forehead and part of the orbital roofs.
question: Which bone forms the forehead?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Forms the forehead, roofs of the orbits, and anterior part of the cranial cavity.
description: The frontal bone forms the anterior cranial vault. It articulates with paired parietal bones at the coronal suture and contributes to the orbital walls and frontal sinus region.
relationships: Parietal bones, ethmoid, sphenoid and superior orbital margins.
study_tip: Identify the orbital plates and coronal suture.
short: The frontal bone forms the forehead and part of the orbital roofs.

name: Atlas
fact: The atlas (C1) is the first cervical vertebra and supports the skull.
question: Which vertebra is C1?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Supports the skull and participates in flexion-extension at the atlanto-occipital joints.
description: Atlas (C1) is the first cervical vertebra. It lacks a typical vertebral body and consists mainly of anterior and posterior arches with lateral masses.
relationships: Occipital condyles, axis (C2), transverse ligament and upper cervical joints.
study_tip: Compare its ring shape with the dens-bearing axis below it.
short: The atlas (C1) is the first cervical vertebra and supports the skull.

name: Axis
fact: The axis (C2) bears the dens around which the atlas rotates.
question: Which vertebra is C2?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Provides a pivot for head rotation through its dens.
description: Axis (C2) is the second cervical vertebra. Its dens projects superiorly into the ring of atlas, permitting rotation of the head at the atlanto-axial joint.
relationships: Atlas, dens, transverse ligament and other cervical vertebrae.
study_tip: Locate the dens and see how it differs from C1.
short: The axis (C2) bears the dens around which the atlas rotates.

name: Deltoid
fact: The deltoid's middle fibers abduct the arm at the shoulder.
question: Which shoulder muscle is a principal arm abductor?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Abducts the arm mainly through its middle fibers; other fibers assist flexion or extension.
description: The deltoid is the large multipennate shoulder muscle covering the glenohumeral joint. Its fibers arise from clavicle, acromion and scapular spine and insert on the deltoid tuberosity.
relationships: Clavicle, scapula, humerus, axillary nerve and rotator cuff.
study_tip: Distinguish anterior, middle and posterior portions rather than treating all actions as identical.
short: The deltoid's middle fibers abduct the arm at the shoulder.

name: Supraspinatus
fact: Supraspinatus is a rotator-cuff muscle that assists initiation of arm abduction.
question: Which rotator-cuff muscle helps initiate abduction?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Assists the initiation of shoulder abduction and helps stabilize the humeral head.
description: Supraspinatus occupies the supraspinous fossa above the scapular spine. Its tendon passes beneath the acromion to the greater tubercle as part of the rotator cuff.
relationships: Scapular supraspinous fossa, greater tubercle of humerus, suprascapular nerve.
study_tip: Look at the superior posterior scapula and trace the tendon toward the humeral head.
short: Supraspinatus is a rotator-cuff muscle that assists initiation of arm abduction.

name: Infraspinatus
fact: Infraspinatus is a rotator-cuff muscle that laterally rotates the humerus.
question: Which rotator-cuff muscle laterally rotates the humerus?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Laterally rotates the humerus and stabilizes the shoulder joint.
description: Infraspinatus lies in the infraspinous fossa below the scapular spine. Its tendon inserts on the greater tubercle of the humerus and contributes to the rotator cuff.
relationships: Scapula, humerus, suprascapular nerve and teres minor.
study_tip: Compare this larger posterior rotator-cuff muscle with teres minor below it.
short: Infraspinatus is a rotator-cuff muscle that laterally rotates the humerus.

name: Subscapularis
fact: Subscapularis lies on the anterior scapula and medially rotates the humerus.
question: Which anterior scapular muscle medially rotates the humerus?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Medially rotates the humerus and helps stabilize its head in the glenoid.
description: Subscapularis occupies the anterior (costal) surface of the scapula. Its tendon attaches to the lesser tubercle of the humerus and is the anterior rotator-cuff muscle.
relationships: Anterior scapula, lesser tubercle, subscapular nerves, shoulder capsule.
study_tip: Rotate the scapula to view its anterior surface and tendon.
short: Subscapularis lies on the anterior scapula and medially rotates the humerus.

name: Teres minor
fact: Teres minor is a rotator-cuff muscle that assists lateral rotation of the arm.
question: Which small posterior rotator-cuff muscle assists lateral rotation?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Assists lateral shoulder rotation and stabilizes the humeral head.
description: Teres minor is a relatively small posterior shoulder muscle running from lateral border of scapula to the greater tubercle of the humerus.
relationships: Scapula, humerus, axillary nerve and infraspinatus.
study_tip: Compare its inferior position relative to infraspinatus.
short: Teres minor is a rotator-cuff muscle that assists lateral rotation of the arm.

name: Biceps brachii
fact: Biceps brachii flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm.
question: Which upper-arm muscle flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Flexes the elbow and strongly supinates the forearm.
description: Biceps brachii has long and short heads originating on the scapula and joins in a tendon attaching to radial tuberosity. It also assists shoulder flexion.
relationships: Scapula, radial tuberosity, bicipital aponeurosis, musculocutaneous nerve.
study_tip: Follow both heads proximally and distinguish flexion from supination.
short: Biceps brachii flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm.

name: Triceps brachii
fact: Triceps brachii is the principal extensor of the forearm at the elbow.
question: What is the major elbow extensor?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Extends the elbow through its common tendon.
description: Triceps brachii has three heads on the posterior arm. The long head comes from the scapula; others originate on the humerus and all insert via a tendon on the olecranon.
relationships: Scapula, humerus, olecranon of ulna, radial nerve.
study_tip: Find posterior arm, three heads and olecranon insertion.
short: Triceps brachii is the principal extensor of the forearm at the elbow.

name: Pectoralis major
fact: Pectoralis major adducts and medially rotates the arm; portions also assist arm flexion.
question: Which broad chest muscle adducts the arm?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Adducts and medially rotates the humerus; clavicular fibers also assist shoulder flexion.
description: Pectoralis major is a large anterior thoracic muscle arising from clavicle, sternum and adjacent costal cartilages and converging onto the humerus.
relationships: Clavicle, sternum, costal cartilages, humerus, medial and lateral pectoral nerves.
study_tip: Follow its broad origin and converging insertion near the intertubercular groove.
short: Pectoralis major adducts and medially rotates the arm; portions also assist arm flexion.

name: Rectus femoris
fact: Rectus femoris is a quadriceps muscle that extends the knee and flexes the hip.
question: Which quadriceps muscle also crosses the hip joint?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Extends the knee and flexes the hip because it spans both joints.
description: Rectus femoris is the superficial central quadriceps muscle of the anterior thigh. It arises from the pelvis and joins the quadriceps tendon into the patella.
relationships: Anterior inferior iliac spine, patella, tibial tuberosity, femoral nerve.
study_tip: Compare its two-joint action with the other vastus quadriceps muscles.
short: Rectus femoris is a quadriceps muscle that extends the knee and flexes the hip.

name: Gastrocnemius
fact: Gastrocnemius helps plantarflex the foot and flex the knee.
question: Which superficial calf muscle plantarflexes the ankle and crosses the knee?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Plantarflexes the ankle and assists knee flexion.
description: Gastrocnemius has medial and lateral heads from the distal femur and joins the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon inserting on the calcaneus.
relationships: Femoral condyles, soleus, calcaneal tendon, tibial nerve.
study_tip: Examine the superficial calf above soleus and trace the common Achilles tendon.
short: Gastrocnemius helps plantarflex the foot and flex the knee.

name: Sciatic nerve
fact: The sciatic nerve arises from the sacral plexus and travels through the posterior thigh.
question: Which major nerve travels through the posterior thigh?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Carries motor and sensory nerve fibers to much of the posterior thigh and most of the leg and foot through its terminal branches.
description: The sciatic nerve arises from lumbosacral roots and typically exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, descending in the posterior thigh before splitting into tibial and common fibular divisions.
relationships: Sacral plexus, piriformis, tibial nerve, common fibular nerve, hamstring muscles.
study_tip: Follow the nerve posteriorly and identify its terminal branches.
short: The sciatic nerve arises from the sacral plexus and travels through the posterior thigh.

name: Femoral nerve
fact: The femoral nerve originates from the lumbar plexus and supplies major anterior-thigh muscles.
question: Which nerve supplies the major anterior-thigh muscles?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Supplies major anterior-thigh muscles and provides cutaneous sensation through branches.
description: The femoral nerve arises from lumbar plexus roots and passes beneath the inguinal ligament into the anterior thigh. It innervates quadriceps and other muscles and gives rise to the saphenous nerve.
relationships: Lumbar plexus, inguinal ligament, iliopsoas, quadriceps, saphenous nerve.
study_tip: Contrast its anterior position with the sciatic nerve posteriorly.
short: The femoral nerve originates from the lumbar plexus and supplies major anterior-thigh muscles.

name: Radial nerve
fact: The radial nerve supplies many posterior arm and forearm extensor muscles.
question: Which nerve supplies many upper-limb extensor muscles?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Supplies many extensor muscles of the upper limb and carries sensory fibers.
description: The radial nerve arises from the posterior cord of brachial plexus, travels behind the humerus, then divides into superficial sensory and deeper motor branches in the forearm.
relationships: Brachial plexus, radial groove, triceps, posterior forearm extensors.
study_tip: Locate its passage around the posterior humerus.
short: The radial nerve supplies many posterior arm and forearm extensor muscles.

name: Median nerve
fact: The median nerve passes through the carpal tunnel and supplies parts of the hand.
question: Which nerve passes through the carpal tunnel?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Supplies many forearm flexors and some thumb and hand muscles and carries sensation from part of the hand.
description: The median nerve arises from brachial plexus cords and runs through the anterior arm and forearm. It passes through the carpal tunnel with flexor tendons into the palm.
relationships: Brachial plexus, pronator teres, flexor tendons, carpal tunnel and thenar muscles.
study_tip: Follow it through the carpal tunnel and identify nearby flexor tendons.
short: The median nerve passes through the carpal tunnel and supplies parts of the hand.

name: Spinal cord
fact: The spinal cord is part of the central nervous system and lies in the vertebral canal.
question: Which CNS structure lies within the vertebral canal?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Conveys signals between brain and body and organizes spinal reflexes.
description: The spinal cord extends from the brainstem through the vertebral canal and gives rise to spinal nerve roots. Its gray matter contains neuronal cell bodies and white matter contains ascending and descending tracts.
relationships: Medulla, vertebral canal, spinal nerve roots and meninges.
study_tip: Study cervical, thoracic, lumbar and sacral levels and distinguish cord from surrounding vertebrae.
short: The spinal cord is part of the central nervous system and lies in the vertebral canal.

name: Heart
fact: The heart drives pulmonary and systemic circulation. This 3D source atlas represents its right and left atria and ventricles as individually selectable structures, rather than one mesh named Heart.
question: Which organ pumps blood through the pulmonary and systemic circuits?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Generates blood flow through pulmonary and systemic circulations.
description: The heart is a muscular pump located in the mediastinum. Its four chambers receive returning blood and propel it through pulmonary and systemic routes; valves enforce largely one-way flow. The source atlas models chambers individually, not a single Heart mesh.
relationships: Right and left atria, ventricles, atrioventricular valves, pulmonary trunk and aorta.
study_tip: Compare atria (receiving chambers) with ventricles (pumping chambers), then study cardiac valves.
short: The heart drives pulmonary and systemic circulation. This 3D source atlas represents its right and left atria and ventricles as individually selectable structures, rather than one mesh named Heart.

name: Lungs
fact: The lungs contain alveoli where oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse between air and blood.
question: In which organs does alveolar gas exchange occur?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide with the blood.
description: The paired lungs occupy the pleural cavities. Air moves through the branching bronchial tree to alveoli where gas exchange occurs; the right lung typically has three lobes and the left two.
relationships: Trachea, bronchi, pleura, diaphragm and pulmonary vessels.
study_tip: Study individual lobes and the location of the hilum and bronchial tree.
short: The lungs contain alveoli where oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse between air and blood.

name: Liver
fact: The liver produces bile and carries out important metabolic functions.
question: Which organ produces bile?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Produces bile, processes absorbed nutrients and participates in metabolic regulation.
description: The liver is a large gland in the right upper abdomen, mostly below the diaphragm. Hepatocytes process nutrients and toxins, synthesize plasma proteins and produce bile that travels through biliary ducts.
relationships: Diaphragm, gallbladder, hepatic artery, portal vein, hepatic veins.
study_tip: Find the liver's upper abdominal location, and distinguish its blood supply from bile drainage.
short: The liver produces bile and carries out important metabolic functions.

name: Pancreas
fact: The pancreas secretes digestive enzymes and hormones, including insulin.
question: Which organ has digestive-enzyme and insulin-secreting functions?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Provides digestive enzymes and endocrine hormones including insulin and glucagon.
description: The pancreas lies predominantly behind the stomach, extending from the duodenal curve toward the spleen. Exocrine acini secrete enzymes into ducts while pancreatic islets secrete hormones into the blood.
relationships: Duodenum, stomach, spleen, pancreatic duct and portal venous region.
study_tip: Distinguish pancreatic head, body and tail and exocrine versus endocrine roles.
short: The pancreas secretes digestive enzymes and hormones, including insulin.

name: Stomach
fact: The stomach mixes food and secretes gastric acid and digestive enzymes.
question: Which organ mixes food and secretes gastric acid?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Stores and mixes food and begins substantial chemical digestion of proteins.
description: The stomach is a distensible muscular sac between esophagus and duodenum. Gastric glands produce acid and enzymes; muscular contractions mix food to form chyme before controlled passage through the pylorus.
relationships: Esophagus, diaphragm, liver, pancreas and duodenum.
study_tip: Locate the fundus, body, pylorus, lesser curvature and greater curvature.
short: The stomach mixes food and secretes gastric acid and digestive enzymes.

name: Kidney
fact: The kidneys filter blood and produce urine while regulating fluid and electrolyte balance.
question: Which organs produce urine?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Filters blood to form urine and regulates fluid, electrolyte and acid-base balance.
description: The kidneys are retroperitoneal paired organs on the posterior abdominal wall. Functional nephron units perform filtration, reabsorption and secretion; produced urine drains through collecting systems to the ureters.
relationships: Adrenal glands, renal vessels, ureter, renal cortex and medulla.
study_tip: Trace the renal vessels through hilum and urine through pelvis to ureter.
short: The kidneys filter blood and produce urine while regulating fluid and electrolyte balance.

name: Spleen
fact: The spleen filters blood and participates in immune responses.
question: Which lymphoid organ filters blood rather than lymph?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Filters circulating blood and supports immune responses.
description: The spleen is a lymphoid organ in the left upper abdomen beside the stomach. White pulp supports immune function while red pulp participates in blood filtration and removal of aged erythrocytes.
relationships: Stomach, diaphragm, pancreatic tail and splenic vessels.
study_tip: Locate the splenic hilum and contrast its blood filtering with lymph-node lymph filtering.
short: The spleen filters blood and participates in immune responses.

name: Right atrium
fact: Receives blood returning from systemic circulation through the venae cavae and sends it to the right ventricle.
question: Which chamber receives systemic venous blood?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Receives systemic venous blood before it passes to the right ventricle.
description: The right atrium is the thin-walled right upper cardiac chamber. It receives blood from the superior and inferior venae cavae and coronary sinus and communicates through the tricuspid valve with right ventricle.
relationships: Venae cavae, coronary sinus, tricuspid valve, right ventricle.
study_tip: Trace systemic blood return into right atrium.
short: Receives blood returning from systemic circulation through the venae cavae and sends it to the right ventricle.

name: Right ventricle
fact: Pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk toward the lungs.
question: Which chamber pumps blood into the pulmonary circuit?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk.
description: The right ventricle lies anteriorly and has a thinner muscular wall than the left ventricle under normal conditions. It receives blood through the tricuspid valve and ejects through the pulmonary valve.
relationships: Right atrium, tricuspid valve, pulmonary valve, pulmonary trunk.
study_tip: Trace the path toward lungs and compare ventricular wall thickness.
short: Pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk toward the lungs.

name: Left atrium
fact: Receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins and sends it into the left ventricle.
question: Which chamber receives blood from the pulmonary veins?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Receives oxygenated blood returning from the lungs.
description: The left atrium forms much of the posterior heart base and receives pulmonary venous blood. It communicates with left ventricle through the mitral valve.
relationships: Pulmonary veins, mitral valve, left ventricle.
study_tip: Locate the posterior atrial chamber and its pulmonary venous connections.
short: Receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins and sends it into the left ventricle.

name: Left ventricle
fact: Pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta for systemic circulation.
question: Which chamber pumps blood into the aorta?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed
function: Drives the high-pressure systemic circulation through the aorta.
description: The left ventricle has a thick myocardium adapted for systemic pumping. It receives blood across mitral valve and ejects it through aortic valve into the ascending aorta.
relationships: Left atrium, mitral valve, aortic valve, aorta, interventricular septum.
study_tip: Compare myocardial thickness with right ventricle and follow the aortic outflow.
short: Pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta for systemic circulation.

name: Parietal bone
fact: Each parietal bone forms part of the upper lateral cranial vault.
short: Each parietal bone forms part of the upper lateral cranial vault.
function: Protects the superior portions of the brain and contributes to the cranium.
description: Each parietal bone forms part of the upper lateral cranial vault. Paired parietal bones meet along the sagittal suture and connect with frontal, temporal and occipital bones.
relationships: Frontal, temporal and occipital bones; sagittal and coronal sutures.
study_tip: Look above each temporal bone and identify the sagittal midline suture.
question: Which structure is described as: Each parietal bone forms part of the upper lateral cranial vault?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed

name: Temporal bone
fact: The temporal bone is a complex paired bone in the lower lateral skull.
short: The temporal bone is a complex paired bone in the lower lateral skull.
function: Protects hearing and balance organs and participates in the temporomandibular joint.
description: The temporal bone is a complex paired bone in the lower lateral skull. It houses middle and inner ear structures, forms the mandibular fossa and contributes to skull base.
relationships: Zygomatic arch, mandible, sphenoid and occipital bones.
study_tip: Locate the external acoustic meatus, mastoid process and mandibular fossa.
question: Which structure is described as: The temporal bone is a complex paired bone in the lower lateral skull?
review_status: Textbook-referenced educational summary; not independently clinically reviewed

name: Sphenoid bone
fact: The sphenoid is a central skull-base bone with broad greater and lesser wings.
short: The sphenoid is a central skull-base bone with broad greater and lesser wings.
function: Links much of the skull base and provides passages for neurovascular structures.
description: The sphenoid is a central skull-base bone with broad greater and lesser wings. Its sella turcica houses the pituitary gland, and several foramina transmit nerves and vessels.
relationships: Ethmoid, frontal and temporal bones; pituitary fossa and cranial foramina.
study_tip: Rotate below the skull to see sella turcica and its greater wings.
question: Which structure is described as: The sphenoid is a central skull-base bone with broad greater and lesser wings?
